questions.answer: Yes. The new byte and its frame-error flag are dropped. The held byte, o_rx_data and o_rx_frame_err stay unchanged.
Yes, o_rx_overrun is 1 for exactly one cycle. It is a separate output port, listed in the port table and in the features, and not part of the receive-stream tuple. It is not qualified by o_rx_valid.
Yes. A frame-error byte is delivered with o_rx_valid=1, held and taken like any other byte. o_rx_frame_err=1 is delivered with it.

Behaviour for illegal values is unspecified and not verified. The elaboration error is only recommended (should). The range 4 to 65535 fits within a 16-bit counter, and the counters need be at most 16 bits wide.
Yes. H=floor(N/2) is the defined sampling offset. For odd N it is a defined point (N=5 gives H=2). No tolerance beyond what follows from the sampling points is claimed.
Yes. Reset assertion is asynchronous. Every flip-flop takes its reset value at once, without waiting for a clock edge. While reset is low, o_rx_valid, o_rx_data and o_rx_frame_err are 0.
Yes. For transmit, the upstream side drives i_tx_valid and i_tx_data, and the block drives o_tx_ready. For receive, the block drives o_rx_valid and the data, and the consumer drives i_rx_ready.
It holds. While o_rx_valid=0, o_rx_data and o_rx_frame_err keep the values of the last loaded byte, or 0 if none has been loaded since reset.
Reset assertion is asynchronous. Release is synchronised outside the block by the environment (ENV-001). The block has no reset synchronizer.
No conflict. The handshake definition itself includes i_rst_n=1, so no handshake can occur while reset is low even though o_tx_ready=1.

A registered output that becomes X at edge E has value X in the cycle after edge E. o_tx_ready is 0 in the cycles after E0 to E0+10N-2. It becomes 1 at edge E0+10N-1, so it is 1 in the cycle after that edge, which is the last stop-bit cycle. A new byte can then be accepted at E0+10N, with its start bit beginning there and no idle cycle.
H=floor(N/2). For odd N it rounds down (N=5 gives H=2). N=1 is illegal, since the legal range is 4 to 65535, so it is not supported. Delivery is at V=M+2.

A TX frame in progress is abandoned. o_txd becomes 1 at once and the byte is lost. A partly received frame is discarded and gives no valid, frame_err or overrun after release. A held byte is discarded.

Yes. Each frame is delivered at its own V=M+2, in completion order. After M the receiver is idle, so the next start is at T0'>M and the spacing between starts is at least H+9N+1 cycles. With N at least 4, the next frame's M' therefore falls well after V.
No. The spec uses transmitter and receiver, with valid/ready streams. Neither master nor slave appears as a role.
The start bit is on o_txd in the cycle after edge E0 (k=0), which is the first cycle after the handshake. It is a registered output, not visible at E0 itself.
Same as Q10.
H=floor(N/2), the offset of the middle-of-bit sample, so odd N rounds down. M=T0+H+9N is the stop-bit sampling edge.
Yes. The frame error of a dropped byte is not reported. In the stuck-low case the spec allows either delivery of 0x00 with frame_err=1 or a drop with an overrun pulse, so it is consistent.
A start bit needs s=1 at one edge and s=0 at the next. A single sample of 1 followed by 0 is enough, and no longer high time is needed.
The spec does not say whether the loopback test is exempt from ENV-004, or whether a delay or falling-edge offset is needed on the o_txd to i_rxd connection. The designer must decide this.
N=1 and N=2 are illegal, since N is at least 4, so they are not tested. At N=4 the sample is 2 edges after the first edge of the bit and 1 edge before its last, so edges just before and after exist.

The spec says the synchronizer structure is checked by lint or structural review. It does not name an owner or say how that check fits into the simulation verification flow. The designer must decide this.
Yes. All flip-flops use the asynchronous active-low reset, including both synchronizer flops, which reset to 1. Reset release is synchronised externally by the environment.
The legal range is 4 to 65535 inclusive. The default is 16.
A byte is dropped when a frame completes at V while o_rx_valid=1 and i_rx_ready=0, which gives an overrun. The frame-error flag of a dropped byte is not reported, so it is not observable.
Same as Q17: M=T0+H+9N, V=M+2.
Yes, both are immediate. On reset assertion every flip-flop takes its reset value at once, without a clock edge. So o_tx_ready=1 and o_txd=1 immediately.
